column4: This is the very sign of Thamud, the she-camel, and the verse says signs are sent as تخويفا, warning that urges caution, as the section explains.
The section names the root ع ق ب in عُقْبَٰهَا as an end and a recompense, then cites this formulation: no معقب can overturn God's judgment.
The section says the Lord who brings the consequence is not afraid of its aftermath; this verse states that He is not questioned for what He does, while they are questioned.
This is the section's cited example: look at the عاقبة of the nine plotters' scheme, which ends in the destruction of them and their people.
The section names ذ ن ب as the root linking sin with an ill end; this verse says each community was seized for its own sin and lists distinct forms of ruin.
The source section itself cites this parallel: Pharaoh's people denied the signs and were destroyed for their sins, making the link between ذنب and punishment explicit.
After they hamstring the she-camel, Salih gives the people three days in their homes and calls the promise unfalse; the short delay makes the stated end measurable.
This is Salih's warning about Allah's she-camel as a sign: leave her alone or a painful punishment will seize them, the same warning-and-consequence relation as in the section.
Salih calls the she-camel Allah's sign and warns against harming her; the section's account of the Lord punishing those who attack what is His grows from this scene.
The people hamstring the she-camel after rejecting the warning, the concrete wrong that the section identifies as preceding Thamud's end.
The earthquake seizes them and leaves them fallen in their homes, giving the punishment following the camel's slaughter a physical end.
Salih warns them not to touch the she-camel with harm lest a great day's punishment seize them, directly joining the sign, transgression, and consequence.
The people hamstring her and become regretful; this is the act whose aftermath the section traces.
The punishment then seizes them; the verse makes the consequence of the camel's slaughter explicit.
God sends the she-camel as a trial and says to await what happens, paralleling the section's sign as a warning before the reckoning.
They call their companion, who takes the task and hamstrings the camel; this is the offense before the announced punishment.
A single cry leaves them like dry brush, a specific account of the enveloping punishment that follows their act.
The verse joins evil deeds and their recompense to humiliation covering faces like a piece of dark night, closely meeting the section's night-as-enveloping-punishment image.
The section defines ذ ن ب through the unpleasant end of an act; this verse says those who earn sin will be repaid for what they used to commit.
The section's account of Thamud's consequence meets this verse's phrase ذاقوا وبال أمرهم: earlier deniers tasted the evil consequence of their affair and face painful punishment.
This verse uses the same formulation وبال أمرهم for the evil consequence of disbelief, closely matching the section's link between sin and what follows it.
The section names ع ق ب as end and recompense; this verse says the disobedient town tasted the evil consequence of its affair and that its عاقبة was loss.
The section says punishment comes because of the people's sin; this verse says corruption appears through what people's hands earned so they may taste some of what they did.
This verse says the evil consequences of what people earned overtook them, a direct counterpart to the section's sin followed by its end.
The section says the Lord took Thamud for their sin; this verse likewise says God seized stronger earlier peoples for their sins, with no protector against Him.
The verse explicitly attributes drowning and entry into the Fire to their sins, compressing the section's sequence of offense followed by punishment.
The section sets the end of sin against purification's success; this verse calls the garden the end of the God-fearing and the Fire the end of disbelievers.
The close wording قد أفلح من تزكى repeats the section's claim that the one who purifies the soul succeeds, giving its positive side a parallel formulation.
The section says God's threat is meant to make people cautious; this verse tells the Messenger to remind by the Quran whoever fears God's warning.
The section reads ukba as a final consequence no one can reverse; here God says His word cannot be changed and He is not unjust to servants.
Thamud are destroyed by the overpowering blast, another specific account of their end after rejecting warning.
The blast seizes the wrongdoers and leaves them fallen in their homes, completing the three-day warning in 11:65.
The section quotes غاشية من عذاب الله for punishment that envelops; this verse asks whether people feel safe from a غاشية of God's punishment arriving suddenly.
The root غ ش و named in the section reappears as the overturned towns are covered by what covers them, a direct image of ruin enveloping its victims.
The smoke covers people and is called painful punishment, closely matching the section's covering language for a punishment that surrounds everyone.
Where 91:15 says the Lord does not fear His consequence, this verse places fear of standing before the Lord in the human being, who then restrains the soul from desire.
This completes the preceding verse's human fear and restraint with its outcome: the Garden is the refuge, a positive end after self-discipline.
After the three-day warning, God saves Salih and the believers by mercy; their rescue marks a boundary between the offenders' end and those who heed.
Thamud deny the warnings; this is the rejection that precedes the she-camel test and slaughter in the same passage.
Beside the destroyed plotters, this verse says God saved those who believed and were God-conscious, the contrasting outcome of heeding the warning.
The section praises one who purifies the soul; this verse draws a boundary against self-congratulation, saying God purifies whom He wills and people must not claim purity for themselves.
The root غ ش و named for the section's night and covering punishment also describes protective slumber here; the contrast shows that being covered can secure rather than punish.
The section's sin-to-punishment link also appears in this account of Pharaoh's people, who denied signs and were seized for their sins.
This neighboring statement makes the moral basis of 8:54 explicit: what befell them was for what their hands had sent ahead, and God wrongs no servants.
This sets up 8:54's Pharaoh parallel by saying those earlier people disbelieved God's signs and were seized for their sins.
Like the section's denied warning followed by punishment, this verse says punishment touches those who deny God's signs because they persist in defiance.
This verse says the person whose evil and sin encompass him belongs to the Fire; it makes the section's unpleasant end of sin a settled destination.

The section follows denial with punishment; this verse supplies the reverse boundary, saying belief and God-consciousness would have opened blessings, while denial brought seizure for what people earned.
This verse states the moral boundary behind the section's outcome: good is for the doer, while evil is against the doer, and God wrongs no one.
The verse connects calamity to what hands have earned but adds that God pardons much, a boundary that keeps the section's punishment from implying every sin is immediately punished.
This verse states both sides of the section's moral outcome: wrongdoers are repaid for what they did and those who do good receive the best.
The preceding verse says a town rebelled against its Lord's command, was strictly called to account, and was punished, completing 65:9's evil consequence.
After the account and loss in 65:8-9, this verse addresses people of understanding with a command to fear God and announces a reminder sent down to them.
After the denial in 54:23, the verse says they will learn who is the arrogant liar, anticipating the camel episode and its outcome.
The water is divided between the people and the camel, clarifying the provision they violate when they later hamstring her.
After the camel is hamstrung, this refrain asks how God's punishment and warnings turned out, framing the next verse's cry as fulfillment.
This verse names Thamud among the peoples who denied the overwhelming event, connecting their denial to the destruction described next.
The verse says Thamud seemed never to have lived there and names their rejection of their Lord, describing how complete their end was.
This is the nine-person plot whose عاقبة the section cites in 27:51: they swear to kill Salih and his family by night and conceal it from his kin.
The next verse says they plotted while God planned against them without their awareness, completing the plot whose outcome 27:51 names.
The plot's aftermath is shown as empty houses because of their wrongdoing, giving 27:51's destruction a visible trace.
The section names ع ق ب for what follows an act; this verse invites the reader to see the end of earlier deniers, the same outcome pattern as Thamud.
The repeated command to travel and see the end of those who denied gives another concrete use of the section's end-of-deniers pattern.
After Lot's people are destroyed, the verse tells the reader to see the end of criminals, another punishment followed by its stated outcome.
This verse tells the reader to look at the end of wrongdoers who denied what they did not understand, linking denial to its result.
The verse says the arrogant rejected signs despite inward certainty and asks the reader to see the end of corrupters, a direct denial-and-outcome pattern.
Here the evil end of evildoers follows their denial and mockery of signs, a close parallel to the section's use of ukba for consequence.
After they deny messengers, God takes vengeance; the verse explicitly asks how the end of deniers was, echoing the section's question about outcomes.
Moses says the good end belongs to the God-fearing, a positive boundary to the destructive end of Thamud and the section's sin-consequence link.
After Noah's account, the verse says the good end is for the God-fearing, contrasting the lasting outcome of heedfulness with punishment.
Those who patiently meet hardship and answer evil with good receive the good end of the Home, a positive use of the section's end/recompense theme.
After the garden owner's wealth fails and no group helps, the verse says God's protection is true and names the better reward and end with عُقْبًا.
The verse reserves the Hereafter's home for those who do not seek arrogance or corruption and says the end belongs to the God-fearing, a boundary to Thamud's destructive end.
This verse describes punishment postponed to a named term and then impossible to turn away, paralleling Salih's three-day deadline and certain promise.
Every community has an appointed term that cannot be advanced or delayed when it arrives, clarifying the time-bound end announced to Thamud.
God does not seize people for every wrong at once but delays them to an appointed term; this makes the three-day reprieve intelligible as a fixed limit.
Many a wrongdoing town is given respite before being seized; the verse then says all return to God, parallel to the section's delay followed by outcome.
The people ask for punishment to be hastened, but its term is appointed and it arrives suddenly, a warning-side parallel to Thamud's three-day notice.
The verse says God delays seizure for what people earn until an appointed term, then leaves no creature; it joins wrongdoing, respite, and consequence.
The verse commands believers to fear God and consider what each soul has sent ahead for tomorrow, making the future consequence of present acts explicit.
This verse says the one who fears will take the reminder, matching the section's account of divine warning as an invitation to caution.
After the purification and success stated in 87:14, this verse adds remembrance of the Lord and prayer as the continuing shape of that successful course.
The verse names the lasting gardens as reward for whoever comes purified, connecting the section's success through purification with its eventual recompense.
Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, putting the section's ز ك و theme beside a ruler who rejects warning and meets punishment.
Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord follows the purification invitation in 79:18 and defines his rebellion before the exemplary seizure in 79:25.
God seizes Pharaoh with exemplary punishment, a clear offense-to-end sequence.
The preceding punishment is called a lesson for whoever fears, matching the section's point that warning is meant to make its hearer cautious.
This verse pairs giving with fear of God, the beginning of a good path and outcome that answers the section's contrast between purification and sin.
The one who gives and believes in the best is made easy toward ease, completing the positive consequence introduced in 92:5.
This begins the opposite course: withholding and thinking oneself self-sufficient, a boundary against the section's successful purification.
The withholding person also denies the best; the verse makes the moral reversal explicit before the hard outcome in 92:10.
The withheld-and-denying course is made easy toward hardship, a direct negative counterpart to the eased course of 92:7.
When the miser falls, his wealth does not avail him; this makes the bad course's end concrete rather than merely naming it.
Punishment covers them from above and beneath their feet on the Day; this is a concrete counterpart to the section's encompassing punishment.
The passage announces visible smoke coming from the sky; 44:11 says it covers people and is painful punishment, completing this row's image.
The section describes غاشية as a covering punishment; this surah opens by naming the overwhelming event الغاشية, whose next verses describe its faces and fire.
This verse begins the description of those met by الغاشية: faces are humbled, giving a human consequence to the event named in 88:1.
The same passage specifies the fire entered by the humbled faces, making explicit one punishment encompassed by الغاشية.
The passage adds a boiling spring for those humbled by الغاشية, another concrete feature of the punishment named in 88:1.
The verse pictures Fire as coverings above its people, a punitive enclosure that parallels the section's enveloping punishment.
This verse says the Fire's walls will surround the wrongdoers, a concrete image of punishment enclosing those who reject warning.
Canopies of fire lie above and beneath people; this gives a spatial form to the punishment that the section describes as covering them.
The verse says the Fire is closed over the people of the left, an enclosing punishment that bounds the section's covering image.
This verse says the Fire is closed over the hoarder named in the preceding passage; 104:9 describes its extended columns completing the enclosure.
The preceding verse closes the Fire over the hoarder, and this one describes its columns extended over them, making the enclosing punishment concrete.
The section glosses ر ب ب as owner and says the camel belongs to Allah; this verse calls God مالك الملك, the owner of sovereignty who gives and takes dominion.
The section's Lord as owner of the camel meets this verse's declaration that dominion is in God's hand and He has power over all things.
All dominion belongs to God and all affairs return to Him; this links the Lord's ownership in the section with its focus on where an affair ends.
